content:
A higher advertised salary does not automatically leave you better off. Compare net income, covered tuition, mandatory deductions, housing and the months for which funding is actually guaranteed.

The 2026-27 comparison table, same basis

Comparisons fail when they mix gross salary with tax-free stipend and forget fees. On one consistent basis — annual support for a standard full-time doctorate, with fees noted separately — the current landscape looks like this: the UK minimum stipend is £21,805 from 1 October 2026 (£23,805 in London), tax-free but with tuition fees normally paid separately by the funder. Germany pays a salary: 65 per cent of TV-L E13 step 1 is €3,094 gross a month. The Netherlands pays €3,204 gross rising to €4,051 by year four. Sweden starts around SEK 30,000-35,000 a month; Norway roughly NOK 550,000 a year; Switzerland CHF 50,000-93,000 depending on institution; Australia's RTP base rate is A$34,315 for 2026 (A$35,550 set for 2027).

Cost of living decides what survives. Zurich and Stockholm consume Swiss and Swedish salaries faster than Leipzig consumes an E13 cheque; a London stipend stretches further outside zone 1; Amsterdam rents rival London's against a lower net salary. The chart normalises monthly support; the table adds fees and duration so you can compare total cost of the doctorate, not just income.

CountryMonthly support (2026)Fees for the PhDTypical duration
UK (UKRI)£1,817 (£2,317 London)Paid by funder3-4 years

Netherlands (cao NU)€3,204-4,051 grossNone (employed)4 years

Taxes, fees and the real net picture

The tax treatment splits the table into two worlds. German and Dutch salaries are employment income: taxed, but carrying employer pension contributions, social insurance and paid leave that a stipend never provides. UK stipends are tax-free but build no pension, and the UKRI minimum is a floor that only applies to UKRI-funded studentships — charity, university and industry awards set their own rates. The Netherlands offsets part of the tax burden with general tax credits; Germany's deduction profile depends heavily on tax class; the Nordics tax heavily but return services. A euro of stipend and a euro of salary are simply different euros.

Fees are the second silent variable. In employed systems you pay nothing beyond a semester contribution (Germany, €100-400) or nothing at all (Netherlands). UK funders normally pay fees separately, but self-funded and some scholarship routes do not, so read the offer line by line: 'fees covered' at which status, for how many years, and what happens in the write-up year. The honest comparison is net monthly income minus monthly rent, with fees as a separate capital question.

Put offers on the same basis

Record the funding amount, currency, payment period and guaranteed duration for each offer. Keep a salary separate from a scholarship stipend because deductions and benefits may differ. When using an exchange rate, record the date and recognise that it can change.

Calculate the costs you must pay

Subtract any tuition gap, compulsory charges, insurance and a realistic housing budget. Include transport, food and the up-front cost of relocating. Check whether advertised allowances are included in the headline amount or paid separately and whether they apply to you.

Compare financial security as well as income

An offer with a higher monthly figure may fund fewer months or leave tuition uncovered. Read renewal conditions, extension support and the treatment of approved leave. Ask for written clarification of unclear terms, then compare the research fit and supervision alongside the financial calculation.

Do not compare gross pay with a stipend

Put each offer into a worksheet with separate rows for gross salary, estimated deductions, stipend, fees and mandatory charges. Keep uncertain net amounts blank until the employer or funding office clarifies them. Add housing and commuting costs for the actual city, then calculate the guaranteed period of support. An illustrative comparison might favour a smaller stipend if it covers tuition and lasts longer, but that conclusion depends on the specific offers. Include supervision and research fit in the decision rather than treating the financial calculation as the whole answer.

Use a common unit before ranking offers

A salary comparison becomes misleading when one figure is gross monthly employment pay, another is an annual stipend, and a third includes a tuition waiver as though it were spending money. First label every amount. Record the currency, payment period, tax treatment if confirmed, months funded and costs paid separately. Only then calculate a monthly budget.

Keep the original currency in your working sheet. If you convert to another currency, record the exchange rate and date, and treat the result as a comparison at that moment. Exchange rates are not fixed for a multi-year doctorate. Your rent and groceries will normally be paid in the host currency, so the local budget is more useful than a large converted headline figure.

A practical comparison table

Comparison itemUK studentship exampleGerman employment exampleDutch employment example
Income basisMaintenance award and funded monthsGross pay, step and contract percentageGross pay, scale and progression
FeesHome or international coverageRegistration and any other university chargesRegistration or project charges where relevant
BenefitsAward-specific conditionsEmployment and social-insurance arrangementsEmployment and collective-agreement terms
Living costsActual host city and housing choiceActual host city and housing choiceActual host city and housing choice
Financial gapUncovered costs and unfunded timeUncovered costs and contract gapsUncovered costs and contract gaps

These columns describe questions to ask, not national guarantees. A scholarship in Germany should be compared according to its own award conditions, and a Dutch external candidate should not be treated as an employee without confirmation.

Work through an illustrative budget

Suppose Offer A provides 1,900 units of monthly spendable income and essential recurring expenses of 1,400 units. The remaining amount is 500. Offer B provides 2,300 units but has essential expenses of 1,950, leaving 350. This invented example shows why higher income alone does not establish affordability. It is not a cost estimate for any country.

Now add timing. If Offer A needs a 1,600-unit deposit before the first payment, you need that initial cash even though the normal monthly budget is positive. Keep startup costs outside the recurring total. Record whether an expense is refundable, whether it must be paid in advance and whether relocation support is confirmed.

Compare the funded period and completion risk

Ask how many months are guaranteed and whether tuition coverage ends on the same date as maintenance. A higher monthly award for a shorter period can leave a larger completion gap. Look at continuation fees, expected thesis-writing time and the process for any extension. Do not add an unconfirmed fourth year to a three-year award simply because another researcher received one.

Supervision and project feasibility also matter financially. A project with the equipment, data and support already in place may be easier to plan than one depending on access that has not been agreed. Ask these research questions alongside the budget rather than treating pay as the only measurable difference.

Are the figures in old salary comparison articles reliable?

Only use them as leads to the official award or pay table. Check the applicable year, contract percentage and deductions. A figure without that context is not a reliable personal budget.

Which country pays PhD researchers the most?

There is no useful single answer for every applicant. Compare actual offers by spendable income, covered fees, benefits, guaranteed duration and the costs of the city where you would live.

Make the comparison usable for your household

A budget for one researcher cannot be copied unchanged for a couple or family. Add the accommodation, insurance, childcare or other essential costs that apply, then check the relevant permissions separately. Use confirmed household income rather than assuming a partner will immediately find work. If one offer provides relocation help or access to suitable housing, record the actual terms instead of assigning it an invented cash value. You can still compare the options without reducing every benefit to one score. State the constraints that matter, identify the figures you can verify and leave uncertain costs as ranges. A transparent comparison is more useful than a ranking based on assumptions hidden in a national average.

Questions applicants often ask

Which country pays PhD students the most in 2026?

Switzerland leads on nominal pay (CHF 50,000-93,000 a year), followed by Scandinavia and the Netherlands (€3,204-4,051 a month in the Dutch scale). Germany's E13 contracts beat UK stipends on gross, while UK stipends are tax-free and come with fees paid.

Is the UK PhD stipend enough to live on?

£21,805 from October 2026 (£1,817 a month) is designed to track the National Living Wage. It works outside London and in cheaper cities; in London the £2,000 weighting helps but many students still share flats or take permitted work.
